title: EKS: node groups, managed add-ons and version upgrades

videos.script: Lesson 9 ran containers with nobody to manage underneath. EKS is the other road: Kubernetes, with half of it managed. {{split}} AWS runs the control plane. That is the API server and the database that remembers the cluster, spread over three zones. You pay ten cents an hour for it, whether it runs one pod or a thousand. {{nodes}} Everything else is yours. A new cluster has no nodes at all. You add node groups, which are Auto Scaling groups that EKS looks after for you. {{addons}} The nodes need software before a pod can live on them: an address for each pod, rules for Services, and DNS. You will see why an m7g.large holds twenty-nine pods, and not one more. {{clock}} And then the clock. Every Kubernetes version has fourteen months of standard support. After that the same cluster costs six times as much, until AWS upgrades it for you. Upgrading goes one minor version at a time, control plane first and nodes last, and nothing goes back. {{moto}} moto keeps a record of the cluster but runs no Kubernetes, so kubectl has nothing to talk to here. Its add-ons and upgrades answer with a 404, and the lesson shows that, then teaches those parts from AWS's documentation.
